steps: Look at the tiles around the gap. Where tiles meet, their pieces join into full circles and long thin spikes.
So the missing tile must finish those shapes at each of its corners.
The gap needs a quarter circle in one corner and two narrow kite-shaped spikes in the two opposite corners.
Only tile E has exactly that, and it also matches the fourth corner.
b2020-1.check: Put E in the gap: every circle and every star is complete. ✓
b2020-1.spot: Missing tiles? Look at what each edge and corner must connect to.
b2020-1.oops: Matching only one side of the gap.

b2020-2.ask: Amira walks from Atown to Betown past five signposts. One sign is wrong. Which?
steps: Wherever you stand between the towns, (distance to Atown) + (distance to Betown) = the whole road.
Add the two numbers on each sign: 2 + 9 = 11, 3 + 8 = 11, 5 + 6 = 11, 8 + 3 = 11.
Sign E: 9 + 4 = 13. That doesn't match.
So sign E is wrong.
b2020-2.check: The road is 11 km, and only E disagrees. ✓
b2020-2.spot: Points between two places? The two distances always add to the whole.
b2020-2.oops: Only checking that the numbers go up and down in order.

b2020-3.ask: Swap every white square with gray and every gray with white. What does the big square look like?
steps: Go row by row. Write each row as W (white) and G (gray).
Swap every letter: W becomes G, G becomes W.
Compare the new rows with each answer, row by row.
Picture D matches.
b2020-3.check: Lay D over the original: every square is the opposite colour. ✓
b2020-3.spot: Picture changes? Write it in letters so you can compare carefully.
b2020-3.oops: Turning or flipping the picture instead of just swapping colours.

b2020-4.ask: 24 muffins. 6 muffins need 2 eggs. Eggs come in boxes of 6. How many boxes?
steps: 24 muffins is 4 batches of 6.
Each batch needs 2 eggs: 4 × 2 = 8 eggs.
One box has 6 eggs: not enough. 2 boxes have 12 eggs: enough.
b2020-4.check: 8 eggs needed, 12 bought, 4 left over. 1 box (6) would be too few. ✓
b2020-4.spot: Buying in packs? Work out how many you need, then round UP to whole packs.

b2020-5.ask: Flora reflects the letter F over two lines. What do the reflections look like?
steps: Reflecting over a vertical line swaps left and right, like a mirror next to you.
Reflecting over a horizontal line swaps top and bottom, like a lake below you.
Draw each reflection of F carefully, checking which way its arms point.
Picture E shows both reflections correctly.
b2020-5.check: Fold the page along each line in your head: the F lands on its reflection. ✓
b2020-5.spot: Reflections? A side mirror swaps left-right; a floor mirror swaps up-down.
b2020-5.oops: Turning the F instead of reflecting it.

b2020-6.ask: Kim joins chains of length 5 and 7. Which length can't she make?
steps: Can she make 13? 13 − 5 = 8 (not possible), 13 − 7 = 6 (not possible).
So 13 can't be made.
b2020-6.spot: Building totals from fixed pieces? Try taking away one piece and see if the rest works.

b2020-7.ask: Maria cuts some of her 10 sheets into 5 pieces each and ends up with 22 pieces. How many sheets did she cut?
steps: Cutting a sheet into 5 pieces turns 1 piece into 5: that's 4 extra pieces.
She started with 10 and has 22: 12 extra pieces.
12 ÷ 4 = 3 sheets cut.
b2020-7.spot: Cutting things up? Count how many EXTRA pieces each cut makes.

b2020-8.ask: Colour the regions red, blue or yellow so touching regions differ. The outside is blue. How many regions end up blue?
steps: Where three regions meet at a point, they must be all three different colours. There are 6 such points.
The outside is blue. Call the other two colours x and y.
Work inwards point by point: at each meeting point, once two colours are known, the third is forced.
Whether x is red or yellow, the pattern always ends with exactly 3 blue regions.
b2020-8.check: If x = red you get 3 blue, 3 red, 2 yellow. If x = yellow: 3 blue, 2 red, 3 yellow. Blue is 3 either way. ✓
b2020-8.spot: Colouring with 3 colours? Where three regions meet, all three colours are used. Work outward from what you know.
b2020-8.oops: Guessing colours without checking every neighbour.

b2020-9.ask: Baskets have 1, 4, 6 and 9 apples. Fewest apples to move so every basket has the same?
steps: Total: 1 + 4 + 6 + 9 = 20. Each basket should end with 20 ÷ 4 = 5.
Baskets with too many must give away: 9 gives 4, 6 gives 1.
Baskets with too few receive: 1 gets 4, 4 gets 1.
Apples moved: 4 + 1 = 5.
b2020-9.check: Every basket ends with 5. Only extra apples moved, so 5 is the fewest. ✓
b2020-9.spot: Evening things out? Find the target first, then move only the extras.
b2020-9.oops: Counting each apple twice (once leaving, once arriving).

b2020-10.ask: A dog walks 3 times as fast as a cat. They start at opposite ends of the path and walk toward each other. Where do they meet?
steps: Count the path in equal little segments. The dog is 3 times as fast, so it always goes 3 segments while the cat goes 1.
While the dog walks the 12 straight segments from P to B, the cat walks 4 segments down the right edge.
Now 4 diagonal segments separate them.
Splitting those 4 as 3 for the dog and 1 for the cat, they meet at E.
b2020-10.check: From E, the dog's distance is 3 times the cat's. ✓
b2020-10.spot: Two things meeting at different speeds? Split the distance in the ratio of their speeds.
b2020-10.oops: Meeting in the middle, as if they had the same speed.

b2020-11.ask: 1 to 10 go around a circle. Any two neighbours add to the same as the two opposite circles. What number goes in the circle with the question mark?
steps: The rule: two neighbours add to the same as the two circles opposite them. So if you know three of the four, you can find the fourth.
Opposite 1 and 10 are 5 and an empty circle: 10 + 1 = 5 + ?, so that circle is 6.
Keep going: next to 1 goes 6 + 2 − 1 = 7, and next to 10 goes 5 + 9 − 10 = 4.
The numbers left are 3 and 8. If ? were 8, its opposite would need 7 + 8 − 2 = 13, too big. So ? = 3.
b2020-11.check: With 3 in place, the opposite circle gets 7 + 3 − 2 = 8, and every number 1 to 10 is used once. ✓
b2020-11.spot: Rules about neighbours and opposites? Compare pairs that share a circle.
b2020-11.oops: Trying random numbers without using the rule.

b2020-12.ask: When Elise leaves, the clock shows 20:20. When she returns, hanging upside down, she sees 20:20 again. How long was she gone?
steps: Hanging upside down, she sees the clock turned around.
Turn '20:20' upside down: the digits flip order and each turns over. It's really 02:02.
She left at 20:20 and came back at 02:02 the next morning.
20:20 to 00:00 is 3 h 40 min. Then to 02:02 is 2 h 2 min. Total 5 h 42 min.
b2020-12.spot: Upside-down or mirrored clocks? Work out the REAL time first.
b2020-12.oops: Thinking no time passed because she saw the same numbers.

b2020-14.ask: Mary has 10 white, 9 light gray and 8 dark gray cubes. Which big cube did she build?
steps: Mary has 10 white, 9 light gray and 8 dark gray: 27 cubes for a 3 × 3 × 3 cube.
Count the visible cubes of each colour (a corner cube counts once, even though it shows on 3 faces).
A and D show 9 dark gray (she has 8). C shows 11 white (she has 10). E shows 10 light gray (she has 9). All impossible.
B shows 10 white and 9 light gray, and the 8 hidden cubes are exactly her 8 dark gray. So B.
b2020-14.spot: Building with a limited supply? Count what you see and compare.
b2020-14.oops: Forgetting a corner cube shows on several faces but is only one cube.

b2020-17.ask: Giorgio has two identical bent wires. Which shape can't be made from them?
steps: Each wire has 5 straight pieces: 4 short ones the same length, and 1 piece twice as long.
So any shape made from two wires must have at least 2 long pieces.
Count the long pieces in each shape. A, B, C and D each have two.
Shape E has only one long piece, so it can't be made.
b2020-17.check: Each of the other shapes splits into two copies of the wire. ✓
b2020-17.spot: Building from pieces? Count what each piece has, then check the shape.

b2020-18.ask: Six stickers on a cube. Two pictures show the cube from different sides. Which sticker is opposite the mouse?
steps: Faces you can see together are neighbours, never opposite.
Write down every pair of stickers seen together in the pictures.
The mouse's neighbours can't be its opposite. Cross them off.
The one left is the dog.
b2020-18.check: The dog never appears next to the mouse in any picture. ✓
b2020-18.spot: Opposite faces? Cross off everything seen next to it.

b2020-20.ask: Three tanks look the same size from the front, hold the same amount of liquid, but the levels differ. What do they look like from above?
steps: Same amount of liquid: a tank that's deeper (front to back) spreads the liquid out, so the level is lower.
The lowest level means the deepest tank. The highest level means the shallowest tank.
Order the tanks from lowest to highest liquid: that's deepest to shallowest.
Picture A shows the tanks with matching depths.
b2020-20.check: In A, the tank with the lowest liquid is the deepest. ✓
b2020-20.spot: Same amount in different containers? Wider containers mean lower levels.
b2020-20.oops: Thinking the tank with more liquid showing is bigger.

b2020-21.ask: What does the frame shape look like from above?
steps: The shape is a frame with 6 side faces, all the same trapezoid shape, with black and gray edges.
Find the one special face: the only one whose two parallel edges are black and other two edges gray.
C, D and E don't show that special face, so they're out. A has a trapezoid with 4 black edges, which the frame doesn't have.
In B the special face is at the top, and going round from it, every face matches. So B.
b2020-21.check: Compare each bar's colour in B with the 3D picture. ✓
b2020-21.spot: Views from above? The top of the object is in the middle of the view.
b2020-21.oops: Mixing up the inner and outer rings.

b2020-22.ask: Three small squares sit inside a 28 cm big square. Lines of 22 cm and 15 cm are marked. How long is the line with the question mark?
steps: The left small square sits on top of the 22 cm line: its side is 28 − 22 = 6 cm.
The right small square sits on top of the 15 cm line: its side is 28 − 15 = 13 cm.
Across the top, the three squares fill 28 cm: the middle square's side is 28 − 6 − 13 = 9 cm.
The line under the middle square: 28 − 9 = 19 cm.
b2020-22.spot: Squares in squares? A square's side is the same both ways. Write every length on the picture.

b2020-24.ask: Two scales balance with triangles, squares, circles and house shapes. What definitely balances the third scale (house + square)?
steps: Scale 1: triangle + house = square + 2 circles.
Scale 2: 2 squares = circle + 2 triangles.
Put both scales together: triangle + house + 2 squares = square + 3 circles + 2 triangles.
Take one triangle and one square off both sides: house + square = 3 circles + triangle.
b2020-24.check: It works whatever each shape weighs, because we only used the two scales. ✓
b2020-24.spot: Several scales? Add them together, then take the same things off both sides.
b2020-24.oops: Trying to find each shape's weight.

b2020-25.ask: 10 scoops: 4 vanilla, 3 chocolate, 2 lemon, 1 mango. Toppings: 4 umbrellas, 3 cherries, 2 wafers, 1 chip. No two scoops are alike. Which combination is impossible?
steps: Vanilla has 4 scoops, all different, so it needs all 4 kinds of topping: umbrella, cherry, wafer and the only chip.
Chocolate has 3 scoops, all different, with no chip left: umbrella, cherry, wafer.
That uses both wafers (one for vanilla, one for chocolate).
So lemon can never get a wafer.
b2020-25.check: Lemon gets umbrella and cherry, mango gets the last umbrella. Everything is used, all different. ✓
b2020-25.spot: Matching with limits? Start with the biggest group; it has the fewest choices.
b2020-25.oops: Starting with mango (only 1 scoop), which doesn't tell you much.

b2020-26.ask: A 3-digit number is 'nice' if its middle digit is bigger than its first and last digits added. Most nice numbers in a row?
steps: To get many in a row, the last digit changes (0, 1, 2, ...) while the others stay the same.
Make the middle digit as big as possible (9) and the first digit as small as possible (1).
Then 9 > 1 + last digit, so the last digit can be 0 to 7: 190, 191, ..., 197.
That's 8 nice numbers in a row. 198 fails (9 is not bigger than 9), and 189 fails (8 > 10? no).
b2020-26.check: 190 to 197 all work, and the numbers on either side don't. ✓
b2020-26.spot: Longest run? Make the rule as easy to keep as possible.
b2020-26.oops: Forgetting that going past 199 changes the first digit.

b2020-27.ask: Magnus plays 15 games. So far he's won 1/2, lost 1/3, and drawn 2. How many games are left?
steps: Won + lost = 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6 of the games played.
So the 2 draws are the other 1/6.
1/6 of the games = 2, so he's played 12.
b2020-27.spot: Fractions plus a number? The number fills the leftover fraction.
b2020-27.oops: Taking fractions of 15 instead of the games played so far.

b2020-28.ask: A 3 × 3 sheet is folded (columns, then rows) so the gray square ends on top. Number the cells so the folded stack goes 1 to 9 from top. What are a, b and c?
steps: Follow the first fold: the columns fold over each other, so each row turns into a little stack of 3.
Then the rows fold, stacking those little stacks.
Track which cell ends up in which layer: 1 on top, then 2, 3, ... down to 9.
Doing it carefully: a = 6, b = 4, c = 8.
b2020-28.check: Fold a paper square numbered this way: the layers read 1 to 9. ✓
b2020-28.spot: Folding a numbered grid? Fold one step at a time, tracking where each cell goes.

b2020-29.ask: A pyramid of balls: 3 × 3 base, 2 × 2 middle, 1 on top. Touching balls are glued at one point. How many glue points?
steps: Base layer (3 × 3): side-by-side touches: 3 rows × 2 = 6, and 3 columns × 2 = 6. That's 12.
Middle layer (2 × 2): 4 touches.
Each middle ball sits on 4 base balls: 4 × 4 = 16.
The top ball sits on 4 middle balls: 4. Total: 12 + 4 + 16 + 4 = 36.
b2020-29.check: Count layer by layer, then between layers. ✓
b2020-29.spot: Counting contacts? Go layer by layer, then count between layers.
b2020-29.oops: Forgetting the contacts between the layers.

b2020-30.ask: A postman visits every island exactly once, from start to finish. He's at the black centre island. Which way should he go?
steps: Islands with only two bridges are tricky: if you pass through, you must use both bridges.
Find those islands and mark the bridges you're forced to use.
Those forced bridges show which way the path must go from the centre.
From the centre, he must go east.
b2020-30.check: Draw the full path: it visits every island once and ends at finish. ✓
b2020-30.spot: Visit everything once? Start with the places that have the fewest options.
b2020-30.oops: Choosing a direction by guessing, then getting stuck.
